pos: n. pl. (what is left on the vine after the vintage; Micah's figure for a nation with no righteous man left in it)
etymology: English grape + gleaning, from Old French glener, to gather after reapers. At Micah 7:1 it renders a Hebrew word for the leavings of the vintage.
biblical_def:
Micah opens his last chapter with a lament built entirely on a farming image: Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit. He is walking through a vineyard after the pickers have gone. Everything worth having is in the baskets and gone to market; what is left on the vines is what the pickers judged not worth the reach. That, says the prophet, is the moral condition of his nation: The good man is perished out of the earth: and there is none upright among men.

The bitterness of the figure depends on the law behind it. Israel was commanded to leave the gleanings deliberately — thou shalt not glean thy vineyard, neither shalt thou gather every grape of thy vineyard; thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger — so that the leftovers on the vine were a mercy, a standing provision for those with no field of their own. Micah takes that generous image and turns it inside out: he goes looking for one ripe cluster of righteousness and finds only what nobody wanted. And then, in the middle of that desolation, comes one of the great turns in the prophets: Therefore I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me. When there is no good man left on the vine, the prophet does not look harder at the vine.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the grapes gathered after the vintage; the leavings of the vine.
webster_full: GLEANING, n. The act of gathering after reapers; that which is collected by gleaning.
GLEAN, v.t. To gather the stalks and ears of grain which reapers leave behind them.
VINTAGE, n. The produce of the vine for the season; the time of gathering the crop of grapes.
CLUSTER, n. A number of things of the same kind growing or collected together; a bunch.
FIRSTRIPE, a. Ripening first; the earliest fruit of the season, accounted the best.
scriptures: Micah 7:1
Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit.
Micah 7:2
The good man is perished out of the earth: and there is none upright among men: they all lie in wait for blood; they hunt every man his brother with a net.
Leviticus 19:10
And thou shalt not glean thy vineyard, neither shalt thou gather every grape of thy vineyard; thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger: I am the LORD your God.
Micah 7:7
Therefore I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me.
corruption_summary: Care for the poor is treated as optional charity, when Israel's law made it a standing claim on the harvest that the owner was forbidden to take.
corruption_paragraphs: The gleaning laws are among the most striking pieces of legislation in the Pentateuch, and they are not charity. The owner does not choose to give; he is forbidden to take. He may not reap the corners, may not go over the vineyard twice, may not go back for the forgotten sheaf, and the reason given each time is a covenant reason: I am the LORD your God, and thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt. What the poor received was not a handout but a portion the law had already withheld from the harvest, and they gathered it themselves, by their own work, with their dignity intact. Ruth in Boaz's field is the system working as intended.

Neither of the modern instincts matches it. It is not a transfer administered by a distant authority, since the gathering is done by the poor in the field of a neighbour who knows them. And it is not optional benevolence dispensed at the owner's pleasure, since he is commanded and the poor have a right. Micah's use of the image is the sharpest possible indictment: in a nation whose law made even the leavings a mercy, the prophet walks the vineyard and can find nothing good at all, and turns his eyes from the field to the LORD.

pos: n. pl. (the cutting of grass; in Amos, the king's first cut, taken before the people got theirs)
etymology: From Old English mawan, to mow. At Amos 7:1 it renders Hebrew gez, a mowing or shearing — the king's levy on the first cutting of the hay.
biblical_def:
The first of Amos's five visions turns on a detail of taxation: Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me; and, behold, he formed grasshoppers in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth; and, lo, it was the latter growth after the king's mowings. The first cut of the hay went to the crown. What came up afterward, the latter growth, was what the ordinary farmer had for his own beasts through the dry season. Amos sees locusts forming precisely then — after the king has taken his, and just as the people's crop is coming — and he knows exactly what it means.

What he does next is the reason the vision is recorded: when they had made an end of eating the grass of the land, then I said, O Lord GOD, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small. He does not defend the nation; he pleads its smallness. And the answer is four words that ought to change how anyone reads the prophets: The LORD repented for this: It shall not be, saith the LORD. A herdman from Tekoa stood in the way of a judgment and it did not come. The same happens with the second vision and the fire. Amos is not a man announcing an inevitability; he is a man interceding, and twice the intercession holds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the cutting of grass with a scythe; the crop of grass so cut.
webster_full: MOWING, n. The act of cutting with a scythe; land from which grass is cut.
MOW, v.t. To cut down with a scythe, as grass or other plants.
LATTER GROWTH, n. The after-math; the second crop of grass in a season.
GRASSHOPPER, n. An insect of the genus Gryllus, that lives among grass; a locust.
REPENT, v.i. To feel pain, sorrow or regret for something done; in Scripture, of God, to relent from a threatened judgment.
scriptures: Amos 7:1
Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me; and, behold, he formed grasshoppers in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth; and, lo, it was the latter growth after the king's mowings.
Amos 7:2
And it came to pass, that when they had made an end of eating the grass of the land, then I said, O Lord GOD, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small.
Amos 7:3
The LORD repented for this: It shall not be, saith the LORD.
Amos 7:15
And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.
corruption_summary: Prophecy is read as fixed prediction and intercession as a formality, when Amos 7 shows a man praying a judgment away twice and the text saying so plainly.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet in Amos 7. The first treats every prophetic announcement as an unalterable forecast, so that the prophet is a newsreader and prayer is decorative. The text will not have it: Amos prays, and the LORD repented for this: It shall not be. The second error runs the other way and concludes that God is genuinely changeable and can be talked out of His purposes by a sufficiently earnest man. Numbers 23:19 stands against that — God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent.

The confessional resolution is that God ordains the means along with the end, and that the prayers of His servants are among the ordained means. Amos's intercession was not a surprise to God; it was part of how the judgment came not to be. This is the standing Reformed answer on prayer generally, and Amos 7 is one of its clearest narratives. The believer who concludes from God's sovereignty that prayer changes nothing has the doctrine exactly backwards: it is because God governs all things that asking Him is worth doing, and a herdman's O Lord GOD, forgive, I beseech thee turned a locust year.

pos: n. (dry feed for cattle; in Job's reply, the ox does not low over it unless something is wrong)
etymology: From Old English fodor, food for cattle. At Job 6:5 it renders Hebrew belil, mixed provender — fodder of mingled grain.
biblical_def:
Eliphaz has suggested that Job's complaining is itself the problem, and Job answers with a farmyard observation: Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or loweth the ox over his fodder? Animals do not complain when they are fed. The braying and the lowing mean something is missing. So, says Job, does my crying — and then he presses it: Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? or is there any taste in the white of an egg? He is telling his comforters that their counsel is the white of an egg: technically food, and impossible to swallow.

The word is worth keeping for what Scripture does with feeding troughs. Isaiah opens his prophecy with a rebuke built on the same observation from the other side: The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider. The beasts know where their fodder comes from and who provides it; the covenant people do not. And the two animals, the ox and the ass, with the crib between them, reappear in the one place no one expected: she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger. The manger is the fodder box. The One whom Israel did not know was laid in the place the ox did.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): food or dry feed for cattle, horses and sheep, as hay, straw and other kinds of vegetables.
webster_full: FODDER, n. Food or dry feed for cattle, horses and sheep, as hay, straw and other kinds of vegetables.
PROVENDER, n. Dry food for beasts, usually meal, or a mixture of meal and cut straw or hay.
CRIB, n. The manger or rack of a stable; a stall for oxen.
MANGER, n. A trough or box in which fodder is laid for cattle or horses.
UNSAVOURY, a. Tasteless; insipid; having no taste or relish.
scriptures: Job 6:5
Doth the wild ass bray when he hath grass? or loweth the ox over his fodder?
Job 6:6
Can that which is unsavoury be eaten without salt? or is there any taste in the white of an egg?
Isaiah 1:3
The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider.
Luke 2:7
And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
corruption_summary: Complaint is treated as the illness rather than the symptom, and Job's answer to his comforters — that animals only cry out when something is missing — goes unheard.
corruption_paragraphs: Eliphaz's method is the oldest form of bad counsel: address the sufferer's reaction rather than his situation. Job's reply is unanswerable on its own terms. An ox lowing over a full trough would be odd; an ox lowing over an empty one is information. The noise is not the problem, and treating it as the problem guarantees that the actual trouble goes unexamined. Anyone attempting to help a suffering believer should sit with Job 6 before he says anything, because the friends were sincere, theologically conventional, and wrong, and God said so at the end.

Job's image for their counsel is worth keeping too: the white of an egg. Not poison — nourishment, technically, with nothing in it a man can taste. A great deal of comfort offered in churches is exactly that: true statements, correctly assembled, with no salt. What the sufferer needs is not more accurate doctrine but doctrine brought near enough to be swallowed, which is why Scripture pairs the manger and the crib. The God whom Israel did not know as well as an ox knows its owner came and was laid in the fodder box Himself.

pos: n. pl. (the seeds of the grape; forbidden to the Nazarite from the kernels even to the husk)
etymology: From Old English cyrnel, a little corn or seed. At Numbers 6:4 it renders Hebrew chartsan, a grape stone — used only in this law.
biblical_def:
The law of the Nazarite is exhaustive about the vine, and this is the most exhaustive clause in it: All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk. Not merely wine, nor strong drink, nor vinegar, nor the liquor of grapes, nor moist grapes, nor dried — but the grape stone and the skin. The law runs from one end of the fruit to the other so that no part of the vine can be claimed as technically permitted.

The reason is not that grapes are sinful. Wine is a good gift in Scripture, commanded for feasts and used in the drink offering, and the Nazarite's vow ended with him drinking wine again. The point of the totality is the vow's character: All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head... he shall be holy. A voluntary, visible, complete separation, marked by hair anyone could see and an abstinence that could not be negotiated at the edges. Samson was a Nazarite from the womb, and his life is the long tragedy of a man who kept the visible sign and broke everything it stood for, until the sign was cut off too. The kernels-to-husk clause exists because vows unravel at the margins, and this one was written with no margin in it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the seeds or edible substance contained in the shell of a nut or in the stone of fruit.
webster_full: KERNEL, n. The edible substance contained in the shell of a nut; the seed of pulpy fruit.
HUSK, n. The external covering of certain fruits or seeds of plants.
NAZARITE, n. A Jew who professed extraordinary purity of life and devotion, and bound himself by a vow.
SEPARATION, n. The act of separating; disjunction; the state of being separate; a setting apart.
VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God; a promise of something to be given or done in return for a favor.
scriptures: Numbers 6:4
All the days of his separation shall he eat nothing that is made of the vine tree, from the kernels even to the husk.
Numbers 6:3
He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink, and shall drink no vinegar of wine, or vinegar of strong drink, neither shall he drink any liquor of grapes, nor eat moist grapes, or dried.
Numbers 6:5

All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head: until the days be fulfilled, in the which he separateth himself unto the LORD, he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow.
Judges 13:5

For, lo, thou shalt conceive, and bear a son; and no razor shall come on his head: for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb: and he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.
corruption_summary: The Nazarite law is read either as proof that Scripture condemns wine or as a piece of obsolete ritual, when it is a voluntary vow whose totality is its whole meaning.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 6 is regularly conscripted into the temperance argument, and it will not serve. The vow was voluntary, temporary for most who took it, and ended with a sacrifice and the plain permission and after that the Nazarite may drink wine. Scripture elsewhere gives wine as a gift that maketh glad the heart of man, commands it in the drink offering, and records our Lord making a great deal of it at a wedding. The abstinence here is not a verdict on the substance but the shape of a particular consecration — and a law that forbade a bad thing would need no clause about grape stones.

What the totality does teach is how vows work. A vow with a margin in it is a vow already being negotiated, and the law closes every margin in advance: kernels, husk, vinegar, moist grapes, dried. Samson is the case study on the other side. He kept the one part everybody could see, the hair, and treated the rest as adjustable — the honey from the carcass, the feast with its drinking, the woman, and finally the lap of Delilah — until the hair went too. Our Lord's counsel about the right eye and the right hand is the same principle in the New Testament: the place to deal with a besetting sin is further out than feels necessary.

pos: v. / ppr. (coming to ripeness; in Isaiah 18, the sour grape cut off before the harvest)
etymology: From Old English ripe, ready for harvest. At Isaiah 18:5 it renders a Hebrew participle from gamal, to ripen or bring to completion — the same verb used of weaning a child.
biblical_def:
Isaiah's oracle concerning the land shadowing with wings pictures a judgment timed with a vinedresser's precision: For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches. The cut comes not at the vintage but just before it — when the bud has set and the grape is filling but is still sour. Everything is in place for a crop, and the crop is never gathered.

The verse before it is the one that holds the theology, and it is easy to misread: For so the LORD said unto me, I will take my rest, and I will consider in my dwelling place like a clear heat upon herbs, and like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest. God's stillness is not inattention. A clear heat and a cloud of dew are both things that work on a crop silently and are the reason it ripens at all. He is watching, and He is choosing His hour. Scripture's harvest language runs both ways: here the fruit is cut off while still sour, and in Revelation the angel is told Thrust in thy sharp sickle... for her grapes are fully ripe. Wickedness is allowed to come to its own maturity before it is gathered, which is why delay is never evidence of indifference.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): growing ripe; maturing; approaching to perfection or fitness for use.
webster_full: RIPENING, ppr. Maturing; growing ripe; bringing to perfection.
RIPE, a. Brought to perfection in growth or maturity; fit for use; mature.
PRUNING-HOOK, n. An instrument used in pruning trees, with a hooked or curved blade.
SPRIG, n. A small shoot or twig of a tree or other plant; a spray.
SICKLE, n. A reaping hook; a hooked instrument with teeth, used for cutting grain.
scriptures: Isaiah 18:5
For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches.
Isaiah 18:4
For so the LORD said unto me, I will take my rest, and I will consider in my dwelling place like a clear heat upon herbs, and like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.
Joel 3:13
Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe: come, get you down; for the press is full, the fats overflow; for their wickedness is great.
Revelation 14:18

And another angel came out from the altar, which had power over fire; and cried with a loud cry to him that had the sharp sickle, saying, Thrust in thy sharp sickle, and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe.
corruption_summary: God's apparent inaction is read as absence or as approval, when Isaiah 18:4 names the stillness itself as the attention of one watching a crop come on.
corruption_paragraphs: I will take my rest, and I will consider in my dwelling place has been read as divine detachment, and the two images that follow rule it out. A clear heat upon herbs and a cloud of dew in harvest heat are not absences; they are the precise conditions under which fruit ripens. The LORD's quiet is the quiet of someone who has set the weather and is watching the vines. Habakkuk asked the same question — how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? — and was answered that the vision is for an appointed time, and though it tarry, wait for it.

The harvest images together settle what the delay is for. Genesis says the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full, and four hundred years passed before it was. Joel and Revelation both have the sickle thrust in when the grapes are fully ripe and the press is overflowing. God does not gather green fruit, which means the flourishing of wickedness is not evidence against His justice but part of its timing. And Isaiah 18 supplies the other side, so no one presumes on the interval: sometimes the cut comes early, afore the harvest, while the grape is still sour in the flower.

pos: n. pl. (those who plough; in Psalm 129, the oppressors who made long furrows on Israel's back)
etymology: From Old English plog, a plough. At Psalm 129:3 it renders a Hebrew participle from charash, to cut in or engrave, used of both ploughing and devising.
biblical_def:
Psalm 129 is one of the Songs of degrees and it opens with a nation looking back at its own scars: Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, may Israel now say — and then the image: The plowers plowed upon my back: they made long their furrows. A ploughed back is a flogged back, the weals running parallel like furrows in a field, and the phrase they made long their furrows means they did not stop at the end of a row. The figure is agricultural and the reality is a whip.

The psalm does not linger on the injury. The next line is the turn, and it is only eight words: The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked. The cords are the plough traces; God cuts the harness, and the ploughing stops. Isaiah takes the same image up to say what no Israelite in Psalm 129 could have guessed — that the LORD would take the furrows on Himself: he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. The back that was ploughed at the pillar in Jerusalem is the one that ends the ploughing, and the healing runs the other way down the same furrows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): those who plow; persons who turn up the soil with a plow.
webster_full: PLOWER, n. One that plows land; a cultivator of the soil.
PLOW, v.t. To turn up, break or divide the soil with a plow; to furrow.
FURROW, n. A trench in the earth made by a plow; a long narrow trench or channel.
SCOURGE, n. A whip; a lash consisting of a strap or cord; an instrument of punishment.
AFFLICT, v.t. To give to the body or mind pain which is continued or of some permanence; to grieve or distress.
scriptures: Psalm 129:3
The plowers plowed upon my back: they made long their furrows.
Psalm 129:1
Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, may Israel now say:
Psalm 129:4
The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked.
Isaiah 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
corruption_summary: Suffering under persecution is either romanticized or explained away, when the Psalms simply record it, name God as righteous, and wait for Him to cut the traces.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 129 does something the modern instinct finds difficult: it states a long history of oppression in one line, refuses to dwell on it, and moves immediately to a confession about God's character. The LORD is righteous. Not the LORD will explain, not this will make sense later — He is righteous, and He has cut the cords. The psalm neither denies the furrows nor builds an identity on them, and a church tempted to make grievance its permanent posture should notice how quickly the Songs of degrees move off the subject.

The christological reading is not an allegorical stretch but the plain progression of Scripture's own imagery. Isaiah 53 takes the same picture of a torn back and assigns it to the Servant, and the Gospels record the scourging in a sentence so brief it is nearly missed. With his stripes we are healed uses the furrow image for the healing itself: the wounds are the channel. Israel's cry in Psalm 129 is answered not by God preventing the ploughing but by God taking it, which is the shape of nearly every promise in the Old Testament when it comes due.
roots_summary: Hebrew charash (H2790), to plough, to engrave, to devise; maanith (H4618), a furrow; aboth (H5688), cords or plough traces.

“he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked” — the harness cut, the ploughing stopped.

pos: n. pl. (those who plant; in Jeremiah 31, men who will plant on the hills of Samaria and eat the fruit themselves)
etymology: From Latin plantare, to plant, from planta, a sprout. At Jeremiah 31:5 it renders a Hebrew participle from nata, to plant — in a promise of restored ordinary life.
biblical_def:
Jeremiah 31 is the chapter of the new covenant, and before it gets there it promises something smaller and almost more moving: Thou shalt yet plant vines upon the mountains of Samaria: the planters shall plant, and shall eat them as common things. Samaria had been destroyed and its people carried off more than a century earlier. The promise is that men will plant vines on those hills again, and — this is the striking clause — shall eat them as common things. Under the law, the fruit of a new vineyard was uncircumcised for three years and holy in the fourth, and only in the fifth year might the owner eat it as common food. The promise is of a settled land, long enough at peace for the ordinary rules of the fifth year to apply.

That is what restoration looks like in Scripture: not spectacle but normality. The verse before it promises tabrets and dances; the verses after promise watchmen calling men up to Zion, and then the covenant itself — I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people. Planting a vineyard is an act of confidence in the future, since no one plants vines for a year he does not expect to see. A people told they would plant on the mountains of Samaria were being told they would be there in five years, and in fifty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): those who plant or set in the ground for growth; cultivators; those who settle and plant a country.
webster_full: PLANTER, n. One who plants, sets, introduces or establishes; a cultivator; one who settles a new country.
PLANT, v.t. To put in the ground and cover, as seed for growth; to set in the earth for propagation.
VINEYARD, n. A plantation of vines producing grapes; an inclosure or yard for grape vines.
COMMON, a. Belonging equally to more than one; usual; ordinary; not sacred or set apart.
RESTORE, v.t. To return to a former good state; to repair; to bring back to its former state.
scriptures: Jeremiah 31:5
Thou shalt yet plant vines upon the mountains of Samaria: the planters shall plant, and shall eat them as common things.
Jeremiah 31:4
Again I will build thee, and thou shalt be built, O virgin of Israel: thou shalt again be adorned with thy tabrets, and shalt go forth in the dances of them that make merry.
Jeremiah 31:33

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
1 Corinthians 3:6
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
corruption_summary: Hope is imagined as escape from the ordinary, when Scripture's promises of restoration are overwhelmingly promises of ordinary life returned.
corruption_paragraphs: A strain of Christian expectation treats the ordinary as the thing to be delivered from — the daily work, the small field, the unremarkable year. Jeremiah 31 promises the ordinary back as the mercy: vines planted, fruit eaten as common food, tabrets, dances, a city rebuilt, children playing in the streets of Jerusalem. The same instinct runs through the prophets — every man under his vine and under his fig tree — and through Paul's counsel to study to be quiet, and to do your own business. When God describes the good end He intends for His people in this world, He describes settled work and a table.

Planting is also the New Testament's figure for gospel labour, and there the same lesson has a second edge. I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase, and then the sentence that ends every ministerial rivalry: neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase. A planter does not make anything grow. He puts a thing in the ground in the confidence that Someone else will do the work, which is why planting is always an act of faith and never an act of control.

pos: n. pl. (a planting of vines; in Micah, the rubble of Samaria made fit only for a vineyard)
etymology: From Latin plantare, to plant. At Micah 1:6 it renders Hebrew matta, a plantation — the bare terraced hillside a vinedresser starts from.
biblical_def:
Micah's first oracle is the destruction of the northern capital, and the picture is of a city returned to farmland: Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard: and I will pour down the stones thereof into the valley, and I will discover the foundations thereof. Samaria was built on a hill, and the judgment is that the hill will be cleared — stones tipped into the valley the way a man clearing ground for vines throws the rubble downhill, foundations bared, the site fit for planting and for nothing else.

The verse before it refuses to leave the cause vague: For the transgression of Jacob is all this, and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? is it not Samaria? and what are the high places of Judah? are they not Jerusalem? The prophet asks his own question and answers it, and the answer names the capitals. The sin of the nation is located in the places that set the nation's tone, and the judgment falls first where the influence came from. Micah is from Moresheth, a village in the Judean foothills, and his book has the countryman's clear sight of what the capitals have done to the country — which is why he can describe the end of a great city in the vocabulary of a man clearing a field.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of setting in the ground for growth; a place planted; a plantation.
webster_full: PLANTING, n. The act of setting in the earth for propagation; the act of forming plantations.
PLANTATION, n. The place planted; applied to ground planted with trees or vines.
HEAP, n. A pile or mass; a collection of things laid in a body so as to form an elevation.
FOUNDATION, n. The basis or groundwork of anything; that on which anything stands and is supported.
HIGH PLACE, n. In Scripture, an elevated spot used for worship, often idolatrous.
scriptures: Micah 1:6
Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard: and I will pour down the stones thereof into the valley, and I will discover the foundations thereof.
Micah 1:5

For the transgression of Jacob is all this, and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? is it not Samaria? and what are the high places of Judah? are they not Jerusalem?
Micah 7:2
The good man is perished out of the earth: and there is none upright among men: they all lie in wait for blood; they hunt every man his brother with a net.
Jeremiah 31:5
Thou shalt yet plant vines upon the mountains of Samaria: the planters shall plant, and shall eat them as common things.
corruption_summary: Judgment is spoken of in general terms so that no one has to hear it, while the prophets name the city, the sin and the class of men responsible.
corruption_paragraphs: Micah 1:5 is a model of prophetic specificity. He does not say that there is sin in the land; he asks what the transgression of Jacob is and answers, Samaria — the capital, by name. He asks what the high places of Judah are and answers, Jerusalem. The prophets consistently do this: Amos names the women of Bashan and the houses of ivory, Isaiah names the daughters of Zion and their ornaments, Nathan says Thou art the man. Preaching that will describe sin but never locate it has learned a style the prophets did not use, and the congregation goes home unbothered.

The other thing worth holding is that the same hills appear in both prophets with opposite verdicts. Micah sees the stones of Samaria poured into the valley and the site left fit for a vineyard; Jeremiah, a century and more later, promises that the planters shall plant on those same mountains and eat the fruit as common things. The cleared ground of judgment becomes the planted ground of mercy. That is the ordinary pattern of God's dealing with His people, and the second prophet does not cancel the first — the vineyard grows where the city was pulled down.
roots_summary: Hebrew matta (H4302), a plantation; i (H5856), a heap or ruin; galah (H1540), to uncover or discover.
roots_lines: Hebrew matta (H4302) — a planting, a plantation; the cleared terrace a vinedresser begins with.
Hebrew i (H5856) — a heap of ruins; what Samaria becomes.
Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, to reveal, and also to go into exile; discover the foundations.
Hebrew pesha (H6588) — transgression, rebellion; the word Micah uses of Jacob.
Hebrew bamah (H1116) — a high place; the idolatrous shrines Micah traces to Jerusalem.

pos: v.i. (to shoot up again; Job's hope for a tree, set against what he fears for a man)
etymology: From Old English sprutan, to sprout. At Job 14:7 it renders Hebrew chalaph, to pass on, to renew or sprout afresh.
biblical_def:
Job is arguing with himself about whether there is any hope beyond the grave, and he sets a tree against a man: For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease. Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground; Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant. Anyone who has cut a stump knows the phenomenon: a dead-looking stock puts out shoots after rain. Job envies it, because his next line is that man lieth down and riseth not till the heavens be no more.

The argument does not stay there. Five chapters on, the same man says the thing he is most remembered for: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth. The book records the doubt and the confession from the same mouth, which is why it has been a comfort to believers for three thousand years. And the image Job used for what a man cannot do becomes, in Isaiah, the image of the One who can: there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots. The house of David was a cut stump when Isaiah wrote it. The shoot that came up from it is the answer to Job's question, and the reason a man may now expect what the tree gets.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to shoot, as the seed of a plant; to germinate; to push out new shoots.
webster_full: SPROUT, v.i. To shoot, as the seed of a plant; to germinate; to push out new shoots.
SPROUT, n. The shoot of a plant; a shoot from the seed or from the stump or root.
STOCK, n. The stem or main body of a tree or other plant; the fixed, firm part.
BUD, v.i. To put forth or produce buds or gems; to begin to grow.
STUMP, n. The stub of a tree, shrub or plant; that part which remains fixed in the earth when the rest is cut off.
scriptures: Job 14:7
For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease.
Job 14:9
Yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant.
For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth:
Isaiah 11:1
And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:
corruption_summary: Job is treated as a book about patience, when its central question is whether a dead man lives again — and it answers.
corruption_paragraphs: The patience of Job has become the whole of his reputation, and the phrase comes from James, who used it well. But the book itself is driven by a different question, which Job asks in the chapter about the tree: If a man die, shall he live again? Everything in the dialogues circles it. The friends have no answer because their theology has no room for the question — on their scheme the accounts settle in this life, so a righteous man in ashes must be a wicked man found out. Job's greatness is that he will not accept their arithmetic and will not stop expecting God to be just, and so is driven to look past the grave for the settlement.

The answer he reaches is not a philosophy but a Person: I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: and though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God. That is bodily resurrection, confessed by one of the oldest voices in Scripture. The tree sprouts because water reaches the root; the man rises because a Redeemer stands on the earth at the last day. Job did not know how it would be done. He knew who would do it, and he said so with his flesh already rotting.

pos: n. (one who gathers; Amos's description of his own trade when told to stop preaching)
etymology: From Old English gaderian, to bring together. At Amos 7:14 it renders a Hebrew participle from balas, to tend or nip sycomore figs — a labourer's job in the lowlands.
biblical_def:
Amaziah the priest of Bethel has told Amos to go back to Judah and eat bread there, and not to prophesy any more at Bethel, for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court. Amos's reply is one of the great sentences in the prophets: I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.

The trade he names is a poor man's work. Sycomore figs had to be nipped or pierced a few days before harvest to make them edible, a labour done by hired hands in the hot lowlands. Amos has no guild, no prophetic school, no salary, and no ambition in the office, and he says so precisely because Amaziah has just accused him of preaching for bread. His whole credential is the last clause: the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go. That is the biblical doctrine of calling in its shortest form. A man does not qualify himself for the work of God by lineage, training, or institutional appointment; God takes him, and the taking is what makes the message binding on the king's chapel.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who gathers or collects; one who gathers fruit.
webster_full: GATHERER, n. One who gathers or collects; one who gathers the fruits of the earth.
HERDMAN, n. One employed in tending herds of cattle.
SYCAMORE, n. A species of fig-tree, common in Egypt and Palestine, bearing a fruit somewhat resembling the fig.
CHAPEL, n. A house for public worship; a place of worship attached to a palace or great house.
PROPHESY, v.i. To utter predictions; to preach; to instruct in religious doctrine.
scriptures: Amos 7:14
Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:
Amos 7:15
And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel.
Amos 7:13
But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court.
Amos 7:1
Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me; and, behold, he formed grasshoppers in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth; and, lo, it was the latter growth after the king's mowings.
corruption_summary: Amaziah's move — this is the king's chapel, take your preaching elsewhere — is the permanent instinct of an establishment religion, and it is answered by a calling no establishment issued.
corruption_paragraphs: Amaziah does not argue with Amos's theology. He argues jurisdiction: Bethel is the king's chapel and the king's court, so this preaching belongs somewhere else. That is how established religion has always silenced prophets — not by refutation but by relocation, by making the pulpit an office of the state or of the donor and then observing that certain subjects are out of place in it. The question Amaziah never asks is whether what Amos said was true, and the chapter is careful to record that he never asks it.

Amos's answer sets the pattern for every faithful preacher since. He concedes everything Amaziah could have used against him — no lineage, no school, no standing — and then names the one thing that cannot be revoked by a priest or a king: the LORD took me as I followed the flock. The Reformed doctrine of the ministerial call has two parts, the inward call of God and the outward call of the church, and the church's part is recognition rather than manufacture. Where an institution has decided what may be said, a man with only the first half will still have to speak, and Amos is his precedent.
